title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: before anything existed: was there something, or nothing?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed aham brahmasmi with the seer Vamadeva: I was Manu, and the sun, and even now. Today a new great saying begins, and it begins inside a family.

Ads love this promise: learn one trick, and everything else falls into place. Usually it's a scam. In the Chandogya Upanishad, a father makes the same kind of promise to his son, and means it. Shvetaketu has come home after years of study, sure of himself, a little full of himself. His father asks him one question. Did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? It sounds impossible. How do you hear what you've never heard?
screen: `LEARN ONE TRICK, KNOW EVERYTHING?` → `A SON HOME, A LITTLE PROUD.` → `THE UNHEARD, HEARD?`

segments.voice: Shvetaketu can't answer. How could there be such a teaching, sir? So the father, Uddalaka, reaches for the plainest thing in any village. Clay. By one lump of clay, he says, everything made of clay is known. A pot, a cup, a lamp: the change is only a name, a matter of words. What's really there is clay. Then copper, and all that is made of copper. Then iron, down to the nail-cutters. That solves the puzzle. Nobody needs to have seen every pot on earth to know what each one is made of. Know the clay, and the unheard-of pot is already known. The father isn't promising trivia about everything. He's pointing at the ground floor under everything. And Shvetaketu, to his credit, doesn't argue. Surely my teachers didn't know this, he says, or why wouldn't they have told me? Please, sir, teach me. That is the frame for the whole chapter. The saying this block is named for, tat tvam asi, that you are, hasn't been spoken yet. When it comes, it will come from a father to a son, after a lesson on clay.
screen: `ONE LUMP OF CLAY.` · `THE CHANGE IS ONLY A NAME.` · `THE GROUND FLOOR UNDER EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `PLEASE, SIR, TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: Rest your eyes on one object near you: a cup, a bowl, a table. Let its name fall away for a moment, and notice only what it's made of. Breathe with that: the shape on top, the stuff underneath.
Tat tvam asi: that you are. In the Chandogya, a father will say it to his son, and he starts with a lump of clay.
Keep this one: tat tvam asi, many pots and many names, one clay underneath. Talk tomorrow.

howItsDone: The sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, Uddalaka's teaching to his son Shvetaketu, is a standard text in Vedanta study, and a teacher may begin it with the clay example.

fork.setup: you're cramming vocabulary, and a friend says: learn the roots and you'll know words you've never seen. how would Uddalaka see that?
options: that's his move: know what's underneath, and the unseen is known.
impossible: you can only know what you've already studied.
a shortcut for lazy students, nothing like the clay.
fork.reveal: know one lump of clay and every pot is known. the father teaches the ground floor under the names, not a longer list.

original.note: Sanskrit: that you are. tat (that) + tvam (you) + asi (are), from the Chandogya Upanishad.

trapdoor: what you thought: tat tvam asi arrives like a thunderbolt.
what it means: it comes inside a family, after a father teaches his son with a lump of clay.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.1.4, vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam: the change is a name, taken hold of by speech; the clay alone is real.

chat.says: a camper's clay pot got squished in arts and crafts. he's sobbing 'it's gone.' what do i say??
options: the pot shape's gone, but the clay's right here. let's make a new one.
be honest: the pot was the real thing, and now it's gone for good.
tell him nothing changed at all, so there's no reason to be sad.
chat.meaning: Uddalaka: the change is only a name; what's really there is clay. The shape can go while the clay stays, and his tears still count.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–7 (Shvetaketu returns from study proud; his father asks whether he asked for the teaching by which the unheard is heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known; by one lump of clay all that is made of clay is known, the change being only a name, a matter of words, the reality being clay; likewise copper, and iron and nail-cutters; Shvetaketu: surely my teachers did not know this; please, sir, teach me)

notes: Block 'tat tvam asi', day 1 of 9 (1752–1760). The text gives Shvetaketu's ages when he leaves and returns; the lesson leaves the numbers out and says only 'years of study'.
The second example is often rendered 'a lump of gold' or 'copper' (lohamani); the lesson says copper. Confirm.
Trapdoor transliterates vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam (6.1.4); confirm the verse number and the rendering 'a name, taken hold of by speech'.
